description: Equipo de estudiantes de Ingeniería en Informática de la FIUBA, con interés en el desarrollo de software, los datos y machine learning.
summary:
Laika finds places on Earth that resemble real sites on Mars. Instead of starting from a famous desert and arguing that it looks like Mars, we start from Mars. We measure three sites (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Arcadia Planitia) with orbital data, and then compare every 5 km cell of bare ground on Earth against each site, variable by variable.

The result is an interactive world map. For each Mars site it shows the 15 most similar places on Earth, how similar each one is on each variable, and where the analogy fails. Analogs that space agencies already use, such as the Atacama Desert, are scored with the same method, so anyone can check that the ranking makes sense.

This matters because field tests of rovers, instruments and crews depend on choosing the right analog site, and that choice is often based on tradition and logistics. Laika offers a repeatable, measurable way to propose candidates, including places that nobody uses yet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Laika is a web page with a world map. You choose a Mars site and the map shows the 15 places on Earth that resemble it most. Clicking a place opens a panel with its overall similarity, its rank, a satellite photo, and a comparison of each measured variable on Earth and on Mars. A switch overlays the similarity of the whole planet as a colored layer.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Mars. For each site we take a circle of 25 km radius and compute the mean and variation of slope, local relief (standard deviation of elevation inside a 5 km cell) and albedo, from the MOLA elevation model (463 m per pixel) and the TES albedo mosaic.

2. Earth. With Google Earth Engine we compute the same variables in the same way on a global grid of 0.05 degrees (about 5 km). Earth's elevation model is finer than Mars's, so we first degrade it to 463 m. Otherwise slopes on Earth would look steeper only because of the resolution. We add aridity (precipitation divided by potential evapotranspiration, 1991 to 2020), with Mars set to zero.

3. Mask. Only bare ground is compared. Cells with vegetation, water or permanent ice are excluded.

4. Score. For each variable, similarity goes from 0 to 1 and falls as the difference between the Earth cell and the Mars site grows. The tolerance is how much that variable varies across Mars. The total is the average of six variables with equal weights: slope, local relief, albedo, variation of slope, variation of relief, and aridity. Each place is scored over a 25 km circle, the same size used on Mars.

5. Selection. For each Mars site we keep the 15 best places between 60 S and 60 N, at least 300 km apart, leaving out the surroundings of analogs that are already known.

RESULTS

Best match for Jezero: Egypt's Eastern Desert (95%). For Gale: southern Peru, near Arequipa (80%). For Arcadia Planitia: the Sahara, near the border of Algeria and Mali (99%).

HOW WE CHECKED IT

We scored known analogs with the same method. Yungay, in the Atacama Desert, scores higher than 98.8% of the analyzed surface for Jezero and 99.7% for Gale. Death Valley scores higher than 99.7% for Gale. The method was not told where these places are, and it still ranks them near the top.

LIMITS

Laika compares the shape of the terrain, its brightness and its dryness. It does not compare radiation, air pressure, temperature, chemistry or rock type. Haughton Crater, an analog used for its impact geology and cold climate, scores low because we do not measure those things. Thermal inertia is shown for reference but does not count in the score, because the day and night temperature range on Earth also depends on altitude, humidity and clouds. For a flat site such as Arcadia Planitia many places score very high, so the rank says more than the percentage. This version covers Mars only, not the Moon.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, rasterio, Earth Engine API), Google Earth Engine, JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet, GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/BautistaBoeri/laika-nasa

USE OF AI

We used Claude, a large language model by Anthropic, as a programming and writing assistant: to compare possible approaches at the start, to write and review the analysis scripts and the web page, to design the page layout, and to draft and edit texts, including this page. All data comes from NASA, ESA/Copernicus and the other sources listed below. No photos, video or audio were generated with AI. Commits written with AI assistance are marked in the Git history with a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line.
